name: Prince's Problem
description: Let the main characters of this problem be personages from some recent movie. New Avengers seem to make a lot of buzz. I didn't watch any part of the franchise and don't know its heroes well, but it won't stop me from using them in this problem statement. So, Thanos and Dr. Strange are doing their superhero and supervillain stuff, but then suddenly they stumble across a regular competitive programming problem. You are given a tree with $$$n$$$ vertices. In each vertex $$$v$$$ there is positive integer $$$a_{v}$$$. You have to answer $$$q$$$ queries. Each query has a from $$$u$$$ $$$v$$$ $$$x$$$. You have to calculate $$$\prod_{w \in P} gcd(x, a_{w}) \mod (10^{9} + 7)$$$, where $$$P$$$ is a set of vertices on path from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$. In other words, you are to calculate the product of $$$gcd(x, a_{w})$$$ for all vertices $$$w$$$ on the path from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$. As it might be large, compute it modulo $$$10^9+7$$$. Here $$$gcd(s, t)$$$ denotes the greatest common divisor of $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$. Note that the numbers in vertices do not change after queries. I suppose that you are more interested in superhero business of Thanos and Dr. Strange than in them solving the problem. So you are invited to solve this problem instead of them.
input_specification: In the first line of input there is one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^{5}$$$) — the size of the tree. In the next $$$n-1$$$ lines the edges of the tree are described. The $$$i$$$-th edge is described with two integers $$$u_{i}$$$ and $$$v_{i}$$$ ($$$1 \le u_{i}, v_{i} \le n$$$) and it connects the vertices $$$u_{i}$$$ and $$$v_{i}$$$. It is guaranteed that graph with these edges is a tree. In the next line there are $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_{v} \le 10^{7}$$$). In the next line there is one integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 10^{5}$$$) — the number of queries. And in the next $$$q$$$ lines the queries are described. Each query is described with three integers $$$u_{i}$$$, $$$v_{i}$$$ and $$$x_{i}$$$ ($$$1 \le u_{i}, v_{i} \le n$$$, $$$1 \le x_{i} \le 10^{7}$$$).
output_specification: Print $$$q$$$ numbers — the answers to the queries in the order they are given in the input. Print each answer modulo $$$10^9+7 = 1000000007$$$. Print each number on a separate line.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 986E — Prince's Problem [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
